newsitem.title: USA: General Signal Q1 woes seen as false alarm.
newsitem.headline: General Signal Q1 woes seen as false alarm.

text.p: General Signal Corp appears to be on track to post solid full-year profit growth even though the company set off alarm bells on Wednesday by warning of lower first-quarter earnings.

Analysts said the electrical and industrial equipment-maker was likely to show improved profits by selling several of its 15 businesses, shoring up its distribution arrangements and expanding in after-market service and support.
General Signal last year managed to deliver on full-year expectations despite a similar stumble in the first quarter, they noted.

"I don't think the outlook is all that grim," said Phua Young, an analyst at Lehman Brothers. "They're trying to reposition some businesses, they're coming out with some new products, and when you talk about trying to do all these things, you're not going to get smooth sailing."

Earlier Wednesday, General Signal's stock opened at 38-1/2, against Tuesday's close of 43-5/8, after the company said it expected first-quarter earnings to fall about seven percent short of the 50 cents a share posted in the year-earlier period. The consensus estimate by analysts was for earnings of about $0.53 a share in the current quarter.
The company said the expected shortfall reflected weakness in its uninterruptible power supply, fire systems and pump businesses.
General Signal's shares edged back to 40-1/4 on volume of 1.65 million shares by mid-afternoon on Wednesday.

"There's reason to believe that the shortfall will be made up as they go forward over the balance of this year," Young said. "It's more of a postponement as opposed to a disappearance of the earnings stream."
Analysts said they were not veering from their full-year earnings estimates of $2.90 to $3.05 per share.
They said Michael Lockhart, General Signal's chairman and chief executive, had in place a new team that was committed to turning the company around.

Analysts said Lockhart was focused on long-term growth and that he had a proven track record. Lockhart, formerly general manager of General Electric Co 's GE Aircraft Engines, joined General Signal in September 1994 and became chairman and chief executive in October 1995.

"Lockhart can improve profits because he is putting in place a lot of the regimes, such as reduction in working capital and cycle times, reducing product-development times, and increasing customer service effectiveness," said Nick Heymann, an analyst at NatWest Securities.
"He's also moving into expanding the after-market service and support business," Heymann said.

"Another catalyst for growth is the company's expected selling off of assets not strategic to the company, and using the proceeds to repurchase stock," Heymann said. He declined to speculate on which assets would be sold.

"We definitely believe that this is one of the most mis-valued stocks right now," said Heymann, adding that General Signal was well positioned to improve profitability by 30 to 35 percent by the end of 1998.
